stories.headline: Update: Todd Blanche Faces Senate Confirmation Hearing, Confronts Epstein Files Questions
stories.summary:
Attorney general nominee Todd Blanche appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee Wednesday, facing pointed questions from Democrats about the Justice Department's handling of Jeffrey Epstein-related records. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) demanded Blanche personally meet with 10 Epstein victims within 30 days. Blanche said he was legally prohibited from directly contacting victims represented by counsel but that DOJ officials were prepared to meet with their attorneys immediately and could arrange such a meeting "as soon as today." He noted the department had already reviewed more than 6 million pages of documents under the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

The hearing produced a sharp partisan exchange over which party bore more responsibility for delays in releasing Epstein records. Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) argued Democrats had blocked Epstein-related subpoenas when they controlled the Senate; Durbin disputed that account, saying he had repeatedly tried to recognize Blackburn for amendments on Epstein flight logs but was blocked by Republican procedural maneuvers. Blanche acknowledged some victim information was improperly disclosed in earlier document releases but said steps had been taken to correct the error.

Separately, former Obama White House counsel Kathryn Ruemmler appeared in a closed-door House Oversight Committee session the same day, facing bipartisan criticism over her years-long relationship with Epstein after her resignation from Goldman Sachs. Emails released by the DOJ showed she met with Epstein numerous times and exchanged gifts with him between 2014 and 2019, years after his 2008 conviction. Ruemmler denied any wrongdoing and said she was unaware of criminal conduct.

The dual Capitol Hill proceedings made Wednesday one of the most active days yet in Congress's overlapping Epstein investigations. The Blanche confirmation hearing carries particular weight given his role would give him authority over ongoing federal probes. The hearing drew coverage from 25 outlets across the political spectrum.

stories.headline: IOC Lifts Russia Olympic Ban Despite Ongoing Ukraine War, Sparking International Backlash
stories.summary:
International Olympic Committee president Kristy Coventry announced last week that Russia will be permitted to return to international Olympic competition, ending a ban that began following a massive state-sponsored doping scandal in 2014 and was extended after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The decision has drawn sharp condemnation from athletes, governments, and human rights advocates who argue Russia has made no concessions to justify the reinstatement. More than 16,000 Ukrainian civilians have been killed since the invasion began, with casualty rates increasing in 2026.

Coventry defended the move by saying the IOC does not want to "hold athletes accountable for the actions of their governments," a position critics called contradictory given that the IOC had already created a neutral-flag pathway for vetted individual Russian athletes during the ban. Opponents note that Russia has not withdrawn from Ukraine, curtailed its military operations, or accepted accountability for the doping program that prompted the original ban.

The decision has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum. Even President Donald Trump, who has sought to broker a peace deal with Russia, has expressed frustration with Vladimir Putin's refusal to negotiate. U.S. Olympic Committee and allied national bodies are facing pressure to formally object to the reinstatement before the next Games.

The reinstatement is seen by critics as the latest instance of the IOC prioritizing commercial interests over political principles, echoing earlier controversies over the 2008 and 2022 Beijing Games. The story was covered by 12 outlets.

stories.headline: Jones Act Waiver Extension Weighed as Iran Conflict Disrupts Global Oil Supply Chains
stories.summary:
The White House is considering a third extension of its Jones Act waiver as the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict continues to disrupt oil and gas supply chains through the Strait of Hormuz. Administration officials met this week to discuss whether to extend the waiver, which currently expires August 16 and allows foreign-flagged ships to transport fuel between U.S. ports. A White House official said no decision has been made but emphasized the waiver has helped prevent domestic supply shortages.

The move faces resistance from within the Republican Party. More than 50 GOP members sent a letter to President Trump urging the waiver to expire, arguing the Jones Act is critical to the American maritime and shipping industry. The law normally requires goods transported between U.S. ports to be carried on U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged, and U.S.-crewed vessels.

The Iranian Revolutionary Guard has threatened to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed until U.S. strikes cease and has also threatened to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key gateway to the Red Sea. Despite the escalating threats, oil prices remained relatively stable Wednesday, with Brent crude at approximately $84.66 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate near $79.25. U.S. Central Command confirmed another wave of strikes against Iranian military targets was launched Wednesday.

The Jones Act debate illustrates the domestic economic strain produced by the prolonged conflict. Energy analysts warn that prices could rise if the Hormuz closure extends further into summer, and the waiver debate has placed the administration at odds with a significant bloc of its own congressional supporters. The story was covered by 9 outlets.

stories.headline: Poland Charges Ukrainian Teen with 47 Counts of Russian-Directed Sabotage
stories.summary:
Polish prosecutors have charged an 18-year-old Ukrainian national, identified as Illia K., with 47 criminal acts carried out between November 2024 and August 2025 on behalf of Russian intelligence. Authorities say the suspect desecrated memorials to Polish victims of the World War II Volyhnia massacre, vandalized the Monument to the Jewish Heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto, and made preparations to fly a drone over Polish President Karol Nawrocki's motorcade during last year's Armed Forces Day parade. He was arrested three days before that event.

Poland's Internal Security Agency said the operations were designed to "incite ethnic tensions between Poland and Ukraine" by exploiting painful historical grievances over the wartime UPA massacres, which claimed up to 100,000 Polish lives. The suspect allegedly acted primarily for financial gain, receiving cryptocurrency payments traced to accounts registered in Russia and China. He faces a potential life sentence if convicted.

The case is part of a broader pattern flagged by Polish security services: the ABW launched 48 espionage investigations in 2025, more than double the prior year, and says Russia has systematically sought to exploit Polish-Ukrainian historical tensions to weaken Western unity. The charges come at a diplomatically sensitive moment, as the issue of the Volyhnia massacre has already strained bilateral ties — Polish President Nawrocki recently stripped Ukrainian President Zelensky of Poland's highest state honor over a military unit naming dispute.

The arrest highlights Russia's continued use of hybrid warfare tactics, including recruiting foreign nationals for sabotage operations inside NATO member states. Poland is a key transit country for Western military aid to Ukraine, making destabilization efforts there of particular strategic concern.

stories.headline: Protests Erupt in Ukraine After Zelensky Fires Popular Defence Minister Fedorov
stories.summary:
Crowds gathered in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky abruptly dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, a 35-year-old tech-focused reformer appointed only in January. Demonstrators held signs reading "Hands off Fedorov" and "Stop sabotaging victory!" as Zelensky offered no public explanation for the decision. Ukrainian lawmakers were scheduled to vote Thursday on confirming Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko as Fedorov's replacement.

Fedorov had been credited with modernising Ukraine's war effort, driving anti-corruption reforms, expanding drone warfare programmes, and using data analytics to improve battlefield performance. His dismissal drew sharp criticism from soldiers and civil society. "This is the worst mistake Zelensky has made during his entire presidency," one Ukrainian soldier told the BBC. Some analysts linked the firing to tensions between Fedorov and Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi; others cited perceived delays in overhauling military mobilisation.

The ouster is significant because Fedorov had become a symbol of Ukraine's high-tech asymmetric warfare strategy at a critical juncture in the conflict with Russia. His ministry played a key role in recent drone strikes on Russian-occupied Crimea, and he had pressed Elon Musk to block Russian use of Starlink — a move that disrupted frontline Russian operations. His removal raises questions about the direction of Ukraine's defence policy as the war continues.

In a Facebook post following his dismissal, Fedorov listed his ministry's achievements and vowed to "continue to defeat the enemy through asymmetry, speed of innovation." The episode reflects mounting internal tensions within Ukraine's wartime leadership at a moment when Western support and battlefield momentum remain in flux.

stories.headline: TSMC Pledges Additional $100 Billion for U.S. Chip Production, Raising Total Commitment to $265 Billion
stories.summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company announced Thursday it will invest an additional $100 billion in Arizona, bringing its total U.S. commitment to $265 billion and potentially adding four new fabrication plants to the eight already planned or under construction in the state. The announcement, welcomed by the Commerce Department as a major job-creation milestone, came alongside TSMC's disclosure of a 77 percent jump in second-quarter net profit to $22 billion, driven by soaring demand for advanced chips powering artificial intelligence data centres.

TSMC chief executive CC Wei said the timeline for the new plants would depend on market conditions. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick credited President Trump's trade and tariff pressure with spurring the investment, noting a deal struck in January that cut U.S. tariffs on Taiwanese goods to 15 percent in exchange for large-scale investment commitments. TSMC produces the most advanced chips used by companies including Nvidia and Apple, making its U.S. expansion a central element of the administration's semiconductor supply-chain strategy.

The announcement underscores the broader U.S. push to reduce dependence on Asian chip manufacturing exposed during Covid-era supply shortages. TSMC is now Asia's most valuable company, with a market capitalisation of approximately $2 trillion and a share price up more than 55 percent this year. The scale of the investment represents one of the largest foreign corporate commitments to American manufacturing in recent history.

The expansion is expected to generate tens of thousands of American jobs, according to the Commerce Department, though specific employment figures and construction timelines were not provided. Wei acknowledged the investment will reinforce the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem and strengthen supply chains critical to both consumer technology and national security.

stories.headline: Update: Genoa Bridge Collapse Trial Reaches Verdict After Nearly Eight Years
stories.summary:
A Genoa court delivered a first-instance verdict Thursday in the trial over the August 2018 collapse of the Morandi bridge, which killed 43 people and triggered one of Italy's worst infrastructure disasters in decades. Fifty-seven defendants — including former executives of toll road operator Autostrade per l'Italia, engineers from maintenance firm Spea, and former transport ministry officials — faced charges ranging from multiple manslaughter to falsifying documents. All defendants had denied wrongdoing throughout the nearly four-year trial spanning 284 hearings.

Prosecutors argued that maintenance was repeatedly delayed and warning signs ignored while profits continued to flow, while defence lawyers contended the real cause was a design flaw in the specific cable that failed and that no maintenance programme could have prevented the collapse since the cable was encased in concrete. Some lesser charges, including document forgery, had already lapsed under Italy's statute of limitations before Thursday's ruling.

Family members of the 43 victims gathered in the courtroom to hear the verdict, describing years of anguish and anxiety awaiting accountability. "After so many years, so many hearings, we may be able to see some light," said Egle Possetti, whose sister, brother-in-law and two nephews were among those killed. Former deputy chief prosecutor Francesco Pinto cautioned that appeals and a final Supreme Court ruling could extend proceedings by another two and a half years.

The case has fuelled a broader national debate in Italy about the condition of ageing public infrastructure and accountability within the private concession system that managed the country's motorways. One defendant, former Atlantia chief executive Giovanni Castellucci, was already serving a separate six-year sentence for a fatal viaduct collapse in southern Italy in 2013.

stories.headline: Pakistan Refuses to Accept Deportation of Rochdale Grooming Gang Leader Released from UK Prison
stories.summary:
Pakistan's government has publicly rejected British pressure to accept the deportation of Shabir Ahmed, a ringleader of the Rochdale grooming gang who was released from prison this month after serving a 22-year sentence for multiple counts of rape and sexual offences against girls as young as 13. Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman Tahir Andrabi told the BBC that Ahmed — stripped of his British citizenship following his 2012 conviction — is "entirely an internal matter of the United Kingdom" and that Pakistan "has no connection whatsoever with this matter."

Ahmed arrived in Britain in the late 1960s and was one of nine men convicted of exploiting girls at two Rochdale takeaway restaurants. Under the Immigration Act 1971, Commonwealth citizens who arrived before 1973 and had lived in the UK for five years cannot be deported, a legal barrier that has blocked Ahmed's removal. The UK government has proposed amending the law so that serious foreign criminals would no longer benefit from those protections, but any deportation still requires Pakistan to formally accept him.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood acknowledged this week that Ahmed's removal depends on Pakistani cooperation, saying the 1971 Act "should not be used as a bar against removal in cases like that of Shabir Ahmed." Following his release, Ahmed was placed in 24-hour staffed accommodation and fitted with a GPS monitoring tag, with authorities warning he would be returned to prison if he breached strict licence conditions. Victims said they were "frightened" and felt "unsafe" following his release.

Pakistan's response creates a significant diplomatic obstacle for the British government, which has faced intense public and political pressure to remove Ahmed from the country. The standoff highlights the legal and diplomatic complexities surrounding the deportation of dual nationals convicted of serious crimes, and comes amid heightened national debate in the UK over grooming gang prosecutions and immigration enforcement.
